Dear all,
I'm conducting a Phenotypic Trajectory Analysis to test how a multivariate phenotype changes between two groups (rural vs urban populations of a frog species) throughout ontogeny (three age groups, inferred from Lines of Arrested Growth).

My question is: Do I need to code the ontogeny as an ordered factor before plughing it into the model in lm.rrpp? The age variable is coded as 1-2y, 3-4y, and 5-6y. I'm running the analysis in two steps, as in the function example:

mod_biom <- lm.rrpp(scores_biom~Local*Age, data = biom)
summary(mod_biom)

TA_biom <- trajectory.analysis(mod_biom, groups = biom$Local, traj.pts = biom$Age)

Thank you in advance,
Diogo

Dear Mathieu,

There are multiple ways to get coefficients from a procD.lm fit: $coefficients, $LM$coefficients, and the coef() function. The former two mean that if you have a procD.lm fit, e.g., myFit, then myFit$coefficients or myFit$LM$coefficients will reveal the coefficients.  The function is better if you also want to perform tests using RRPP; e.g.,

coef(myFit) # reveals coefficients
coef(myFit, test = TRUE) # performs test on coefficients

Hope this helps!

Mike

messages.subject: Simulating random data/landmarks around mean shapes + Identifying covariances introduced by GPA or combine.subsets
messages.subject_clean: Simulating random data/landmarks around mean shapes + Identifying covariances introduced by GPA or combine.subsets
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I’m hoping to get some help on two questions.
I’ve thought about them a lot and am feeling stuck.

First, the questions:
How (practically) could I simulate random data/landmarks around mean shapes?
More conceptually, could I use the data from Q1 to identify and account for covariance biases in a modularity analysis (using phylo.modularity) that might be introduced by performing GPAs on individual bones and then combining them with combine.subsets (without a second GPA during combine subsets).

Second, the background to these questions:
We recently had a paper reviewed where we performed GPAs on individual bones(vertebrae) for many species. After each vertebrae was aligned for all species, we then combined those vertebrae with combine.subsets. We did not perform a second GPA during implementation of combine.subset function (option GPA = FALSE), so that vertebrae were equally scaled in our analysis and to avoid introducing covariances that can mislead modularity analyses when modules are subsets of a common Procrustes superimposition (Cardini 2019).
Cardini, A. (2019). Integration and modularity in Procrustes shape data: is there a risk of spurious results?. Evolutionary Biology, 46(1), 90-105.

However, Cardini (2019) also pointed out that “the separate blocks approach may have appropriate rates of type I errors (no more false positives than expected by chance because of sampling error), but yet lead to large type II error rates (i.e., too many false negatives suggesting no integration when in fact it is there).”
Thus, Cardini speculates that although our chosen analysis avoids the pitfalls evidenced in their study, our analysis may have issues that they did not analytically explore.

A reviewer pointed out “the potential for covariances to be introduced by the superimposition (or even just the spacing of the landmarks). There may also be covariances introduced or removed by the combine.subsets function.”

And they suggested “that you simulate random data around the mean shapes, and run the analyses of modularity on those data, to determine whether those too yield an apparently modular signal like the one you discerned in your data. I found that all the models that I fit were favored over the null, and some models were also favored over others when fit to the simulated data.  If you also find that covariances are introduced by superimposition, and either introduced or removed by combining subsets, you might reconsider what the appropriate null hypothesis should be when testing for modularity.”

However, I’m having trouble figuring out 1) how to simulate the data and 2) whether and how I could use those simulated data to find a more “appropriate null hypothesis”. Cardini (2019) identified biases using many datasets and I would just be simulating data around my single example dataset. Is this even sufficient? Or should I just be providing clear caveats and explanations of this potential biases in our discussion?

I realize this is a larger question that might go beyond the scope of this group. But I’m curious if anyone has performed similar simulations or has ideas on how to test for these biases and interpret the results.

For those that made it this far in the message, THANK YOU for your consideration.
I really appreciate any ideas/help.

I’m happy to clarify anything via group messages or by any other chat method.

Dear geomorph community,

I am conducting a phenotypic trajectory analysis to investigate possible intraspecific sexual shape dimorphism in fish species inhabiting two different areas in the Adriatic Sea that differ mainly in terms of resource availability and structure. However, I am also interested in examining sexual size dimorphism between the sampled populations and whether they follow Rensch's rule or the pattern whereby size is more female biased (i.e., the female size to male size ratio is higher) the smaller the body size of the species, whereas it becomes increasingly more male biased the larger-bodied the species.

I came across the angler package (https://github.com/TWilliamBell/angler), which seems to be compatible with geomorph as it provides the ability to calculate sexual size and shape dimorphism using landmark-based sexual dimorphism data. However, I have not been able to run the code or structure it properly. So, I was wondering if anyone has experience with this package and can provide some guidelines on how to implement the code with geomorph.

Also, if someone has some advice how to produce the RMA analysis and the plot as found in Kelly et al. (2013) – Figure 4 would be helpful, as I have difficulties  creating it properly due to insufficient coding skills.

 Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

Igor

Reference:

Kelly, C.D., Folinsbee, K.E., Adams, D.C., Jennions, M.,D. (2013) Intraspecific sexual size and shape dimorphism in an Australian freshwater fish differs with respect to a biogeographic barrier and latitude. Evolutionary Biology, 40: 408-419.

Molly,

Your post hits upon an area for which considerable theoretical work is still required: Cardini 2019 is hardly the last word on the subject. In fact, just last week I was diving into conceptual issues related to the broader topic for which said paper only superficially glances at. Hopefully my deep-dive will turn up something of a more general solution to the broader set of problems here (there are several, not just ‘separate’ GPA vs. single), but that will take a while for me to sort out. In the meantime, to help you move forward with your particular empirical study, here are a few thoughts that may be helpful.

First, I totally agree that when one has several empirical moving parts, it is a good idea to simulate some data, so that you can control for one aspect of the study (true landmark variation/covariation) while examining the effects of another (e.g., landmark spacing or other components).  The procedure you outlines is on the right track: simulate data around the mean shape to generate a ‘sample’ of representative observations, which are then used in some down-stream pipeline.  A script to do this is below.

NOTE: a very important step – and one that some folks often miss or otherwise do not appreciate – is the scaling of the random input variation relative to the size of your object matters a great deal.  One has to get this just right, or any analysis, type I error, type II error test, etc. is simply GIGO (garbage-in-garbage-out).  As your simulations are based on your empirical study, I recommend scaling the random variation you generate by the observed variation in your sample.

In the script below, I do it both ways: first the naïve simulation where the scaling step is ignored, and then with scaling relative to actual total variation. The plots make the difference blindingly obvious.

###

library(geomorph)

library(MASS)

data(plethodon)

manders <- gpagen(plethodon$land)

mn <- mshape(manders$coords)

n <-dim(plethodon$land)[3]

p <- manders$p; k <- manders$k

var.obs <- mean(diag(var(two.d.array(manders$coords))))  #average landmark-coordinate variation in observed data

sim.1 <- arrayspecs(mvrnorm(n,mu=matrix(t(mn)),Sigma=diag(1,p*k)),p=p,k=k)   #naive simulation

sim.2 <- arrayspecs(mvrnorm(n,mu=matrix(t(mn)),Sigma=diag(var.obs,p*k)),p=p,k=k)   #variance-informed simulation

plotAllSpecimens(sim.1)

plotAllSpecimens(sim.2)

###

Good luck with your study!!!

Dean

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Hi all,
I’m hoping to get some help on two questions.
I’ve thought about them a lot and am feeling stuck.

First, the questions:
How (practically) could I simulate random data/landmarks around mean shapes?
More conceptually, could I use the data from Q1 to identify and account for covariance biases in a modularity analysis (using phylo.modularity) that might be introduced by performing GPAs on individual bones and then combining them with combine.subsets (without a second GPA during combine subsets).

Second, the background to these questions:
We recently had a paper reviewed where we performed GPAs on individual bones(vertebrae) for many species. After each vertebrae was aligned for all species, we then combined those vertebrae with combine.subsets. We did not perform a second GPA during implementation of combine.subset function (option GPA = FALSE), so that vertebrae were equally scaled in our analysis and to avoid introducing covariances that can mislead modularity analyses when modules are subsets of a common Procrustes superimposition (Cardini 2019).
Cardini, A. (2019). Integration and modularity in Procrustes shape data: is there a risk of spurious results?. Evolutionary Biology, 46(1), 90-105.

However, Cardini (2019) also pointed out that “the separate blocks approach may have appropriate rates of type I errors (no more false positives than expected by chance because of sampling error), but yet lead to large type II error rates (i.e., too many false negatives suggesting no integration when in fact it is there).”
Thus, Cardini speculates that although our chosen analysis avoids the pitfalls evidenced in their study, our analysis may have issues that they did not analytically explore.

A reviewer pointed out “the potential for covariances to be introduced by the superimposition (or even just the spacing of the landmarks). There may also be covariances introduced or removed by the combine.subsets function.”

And they suggested “that you simulate random data around the mean shapes, and run the analyses of modularity on those data, to determine whether those too yield an apparently modular signal like the one you discerned in your data. I found that all the models that I fit were favored over the null, and some models were also favored over others when fit to the simulated data.  If you also find that covariances are introduced by superimposition, and either introduced or removed by combining subsets, you might reconsider what the appropriate null hypothesis should be when testing for modularity.”

However, I’m having trouble figuring out 1) how to simulate the data and 2) whether and how I could use those simulated data to find a more “appropriate null hypothesis”. Cardini (2019) identified biases using many datasets and I would just be simulating data around my single example dataset. Is this even sufficient? Or should I just be providing clear caveats and explanations of this potential biases in our discussion?

I realize this is a larger question that might go beyond the scope of this group. But I’m curious if anyone has performed similar simulations or has ideas on how to test for these biases and interpret the results.

For those that made it this far in the message, THANK YOU for your consideration.
I really appreciate any ideas/help.

I’m happy to clarify anything via group messages or by any other chat method.

The goal here is to create many modularity outcomes, assuming the covariances within modules are due to nothing more than GPA.  CAVEATS: I have not given a lot of thought to the appropriateness of this as a method but merely suggest it as an aid for simulating random data.  Also, by using verbose = TRUE in gpagen, it is possible to skip a couple of steps that Dean suggested, as it creates a covariance matrix for different points.  (Also Dean used the mean of variances to apply to all points.  I use each point's variances.  Neither is correct nor incorrect, without additional research.  Getting these variances post-GPA and then simulating data on which GPA will again be performed makes this process a little challenging.)

Script below - Mike

# Using plethspecies example:

library(geomorph)
data(plethspecies)
Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethspecies$land, verbose = TRUE)    # verbose = TRUE, provides VCV
land.gps<-c("A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B")

MT <- phylo.modularity(Y.gpa$coords, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=land.gps,
                       phy=plethspecies$phy,
                       CI = FALSE, iter=999)
summary(MT) # Test summary

Mean <- Y.gpa$consensus # mean config
Mean.vect <- as.vector(t(Mean)) # make the mean into a vector
Var <- diag(diag(Y.gpa$points.VCV)) # Isotropic variances from GPA VCV
n <- length(Y.gpa$Csize)
p <- Y.gpa$p
k <- Y.gpa$k

# One permutation of random data:
library(MASS)

IsoCoords <- mvrnorm(n, mu = Mean.vect, Sigma = Var)
IsoCoords <- arrayspecs(IsoCoords, p, k)

# These should look nearly indistinguishable:

plotAllSpecimens(Y.gpa$coords, plot.param = list(mean.cex = 0.5))
dimnames(IsoCoords) <- dimnames(Y.gpa$coords)
Y.gpar <- gpagen(IsoCoords)
plotAllSpecimens(Y.gpar$coords, plot.param = list(mean.cex = 0.5))

MTr <- phylo.modularity(Y.gpar$coords, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=land.gps,
                       phy=plethspecies$phy,
                       CI = FALSE, iter=999)
summary(MTr)

# A function for multiple permutations of isotropic data
# This will make a list of random permutations
# This expects that GPA was performed with verbose = TRUE

makeIsoCoords <- function(GPA, permutations){
  coords <- GPA$coords
  n <- length(GPA$Csize)
  p <- GPA$p
  k <- GPA$k
  Mean <- GPA$consensus # mean config
  Mean.vect <- as.vector(t(Mean)) # make the mean into a vector
  Var <- diag(diag(GPA$points.VCV)) # Isotropic variances from GPA VCV
  result <- lapply(1:permutations, function(.){
    IsoCoords <- mvrnorm(n, mu = Mean.vect, Sigma = Var)
    IsoCoords <- arrayspecs(IsoCoords, p, k)
    GPAr <- gpagen(IsoCoords, print.progress = FALSE)
    rCoords <- GPAr$coords
    dimnames(rCoords) <- dimnames(GPA$coords)
    rCoords
  })

  return(result)
}

# Example for how to get 100 effect sizes from random data:

randomCoords <- makeIsoCoords(Y.gpa, 100)

getZ <- function(coords){
  MT <- phylo.modularity(coords, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=land.gps,
                         phy=plethspecies$phy,
                         CI = FALSE, iter=999, print.progress = FALSE)
  return(MT$Z)
}

Zs <- sapply(randomCoords, getZ) # get 100 Z scores

summary(Zs) # make a five-point summary of the Zs

# from random data, it would suggest the effect is not merely due to GPA, per Cardini

Hi all,

Igor, I just wanted to share the following code since it is published, which would help in the review process (not to discourage angler - I am excited to see what it can do). This is the paper https://doi.org/10.1111/evo.14049 and the associated code is in Dryad here https://datadryad.org/stash/downloads/file_stream/531722. The code is easy to follow and I am using it in one of my projects as well.

Regarding use of RMA in testing for patterns of allometry in sexual dimorphism, the latter paper describes why it might not be a good approach. Further explanation is given here (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10682-021-10132-x), please message me individually if you need a copy. We justify the use of OLS for our dataset, and verify those results using phylogenetic regression while incorporating sampling error (http://www.phytools.org/static.help/pgls.Ives.html). It might be worth thinking about whether this is a useful approach for you.

Best,
Bryan

On Thursday, July 14, 2022 at 9:09:44 AM UTC-5 mlco...@gmail.com wrote:
> Dear Molly,
>
> I was in the process of providing an example when Dean beat me to it, but I’ll provide mine, anyway, because it has a step to not only create random data but create many sets of random data, from which one might create a distribution of modularity effect sizes created from isotropic data.  The goal here is to create many modularity outcomes, assuming the covariances within modules are due to nothing more than GPA.  CAVEATS: I have not given a lot of thought to the appropriateness of this as a method but merely suggest it as an aid for simulating random data.  Also, by using verbose = TRUE in gpagen, it is possible to skip a couple of steps that Dean suggested, as it creates a covariance matrix for different points.  (Also Dean used the mean of variances to apply to all points.  I use each point's variances.  Neither is correct nor incorrect, without additional research.  Getting these variances post-GPA and then simulating data on which GPA will again be performed makes this process a little challenging.)
>
> Script below - Mike
>
> # Using plethspecies example:
>
> library(geomorph)
> data(plethspecies)
> Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethspecies$land, verbose = TRUE)    # verbose = TRUE, provides VCV
> land.gps<-c("A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B")
>
> MT <- phylo.modularity(Y.gpa$coords, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=land.gps,
>                        phy=plethspecies$phy,
>                        CI = FALSE, iter=999)
> summary(MT) # Test summary
>
> Mean <- Y.gpa$consensus # mean config
> Mean.vect <- as.vector(t(Mean)) # make the mean into a vector
> Var <- diag(diag(Y.gpa$points.VCV)) # Isotropic variances from GPA VCV
> n <- length(Y.gpa$Csize)
> p <- Y.gpa$p
> k <- Y.gpa$k
>
> # One permutation of random data:
> library(MASS)
>
> IsoCoords <- mvrnorm(n, mu = Mean.vect, Sigma = Var)
> IsoCoords <- arrayspecs(IsoCoords, p, k)
>
> # These should look nearly indistinguishable:
>
> plotAllSpecimens(Y.gpa$coords, plot.param = list(mean.cex = 0.5))
> dimnames(IsoCoords) <- dimnames(Y.gpa$coords)
> Y.gpar <- gpagen(IsoCoords)
> plotAllSpecimens(Y.gpar$coords, plot.param = list(mean.cex = 0.5))
>
> # Modularity test done on isotropic random data
>
> MTr <- phylo.modularity(Y.gpar$coords, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=land.gps,
>                        phy=plethspecies$phy,
>                        CI = FALSE, iter=999)
> summary(MTr)
>
> # A function for multiple permutations of isotropic data
> # This will make a list of random permutations
> # This expects that GPA was performed with verbose = TRUE
>
> makeIsoCoords <- function(GPA, permutations){
>   coords <- GPA$coords
>   n <- length(GPA$Csize)
>   p <- GPA$p
>   k <- GPA$k
>   Mean <- GPA$consensus # mean config
>   Mean.vect <- as.vector(t(Mean)) # make the mean into a vector
>   Var <- diag(diag(GPA$points.VCV)) # Isotropic variances from GPA VCV
>   result <- lapply(1:permutations, function(.){
>     IsoCoords <- mvrnorm(n, mu = Mean.vect, Sigma = Var)
>     IsoCoords <- arrayspecs(IsoCoords, p, k)
>     GPAr <- gpagen(IsoCoords, print.progress = FALSE)
>     rCoords <- GPAr$coords
>     dimnames(rCoords) <- dimnames(GPA$coords)
>     rCoords
>   })
>
>   return(result)
> }
>
> # Example for how to get 100 effect sizes from random data:
>
> randomCoords <- makeIsoCoords(Y.gpa, 100)
>
> getZ <- function(coords){
>   MT <- phylo.modularity(coords, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=land.gps,
>                          phy=plethspecies$phy,
>                          CI = FALSE, iter=999, print.progress = FALSE)
>   return(MT$Z)
> }
>
> Zs <- sapply(randomCoords, getZ) # get 100 Z scores
>
> summary(Zs) # make a five-point summary of the Zs
>
> # One could compare their observed result to the distribution of Zs made from isotropic data
> # If modularity is more pronounced in the observed case than what is commonly generated
> # from random data, it would suggest the effect is not merely due to GPA, per Cardini
>

> > On Jul 14, 2022, at 8:56 AM, Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Molly,
> >
> > Your post hits upon an area for which considerable theoretical work is still required: Cardini 2019 is hardly the last word on the subject. In fact, just last week I was diving into conceptual issues related to the broader topic for which said paper only superficially glances at. Hopefully my deep-dive will turn up something of a more general solution to the broader set of problems here (there are several, not just ‘separate’ GPA vs. single), but that will take a while for me to sort out. In the meantime, to help you move forward with your particular empirical study, here are a few thoughts that may be helpful.
> >
> > First, I totally agree that when one has several empirical moving parts, it is a good idea to simulate some data, so that you can control for one aspect of the study (true landmark variation/covariation) while examining the effects of another (e.g., landmark spacing or other components).  The procedure you outlines is on the right track: simulate data around the mean shape to generate a ‘sample’ of representative observations, which are then used in some down-stream pipeline.  A script to do this is below.
> >
> > NOTE: a very important step – and one that some folks often miss or otherwise do not appreciate – is the scaling of the random input variation relative to the size of your object matters a great deal.  One has to get this just right, or any analysis, type I error, type II error test, etc. is simply GIGO (garbage-in-garbage-out).  As your simulations are based on your empirical study, I recommend scaling the random variation you generate by the observed variation in your sample.
> >
> > In the script below, I do it both ways: first the naïve simulation where the scaling step is ignored, and then with scaling relative to actual total variation. The plots make the difference blindingly obvious.
> >
> > ###
> > library(geomorph)
> > library(MASS)
> >
> > data(plethodon)
> > manders <- gpagen(plethodon$land)
> > mn <- mshape(manders$coords)
> > n <-dim(plethodon$land)[3]
> > p <- manders$p; k <- manders$k
> >
> > var.obs <- mean(diag(var(two.d.array(manders$coords))))  #average landmark-coordinate variation in observed data
> >
> > sim.1 <- arrayspecs(mvrnorm(n,mu=matrix(t(mn)),Sigma=diag(1,p*k)),p=p,k=k)   #naive simulation
> > sim.2 <- arrayspecs(mvrnorm(n,mu=matrix(t(mn)),Sigma=diag(var.obs,p*k)),p=p,k=k)   #variance-informed simulation
> >
> > plotAllSpecimens(sim.1)
> > plotAllSpecimens(sim.2)
> > ###
> >
> > Good luck with your study!!!
> >
> > Dean
> >

> > Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

> > Hi all,

> > I’ve thought about them a lot and am feeling stuck.
> >
> > First, the questions:
> > How (practically) could I simulate random data/landmarks around mean shapes?
> > More conceptually, could I use the data from Q1 to identify and account for covariance biases in a modularity analysis (using phylo.modularity) that might be introduced by performing GPAs on individual bones and then combining them with combine.subsets (without a second GPA during combine subsets).
> >
> > Second, the background to these questions:
> > We recently had a paper reviewed where we performed GPAs on individual bones(vertebrae) for many species. After each vertebrae was aligned for all species, we then combined those vertebrae with combine.subsets. We did not perform a second GPA during implementation of combine.subset function (option GPA = FALSE), so that vertebrae were equally scaled in our analysis and to avoid introducing covariances that can mislead modularity analyses when modules are subsets of a common Procrustes superimposition (Cardini 2019).
> > Cardini, A. (2019). Integration and modularity in Procrustes shape data: is there a risk of spurious results?. Evolutionary Biology, 46(1), 90-105.
> >
> > However, Cardini (2019) also pointed out that “the separate blocks approach may have appropriate rates of type I errors (no more false positives than expected by chance because of sampling error), but yet lead to large type II error rates (i.e., too many false negatives suggesting no integration when in fact it is there).”
> > Thus, Cardini speculates that although our chosen analysis avoids the pitfalls evidenced in their study, our analysis may have issues that they did not analytically explore.
> >
> > A reviewer pointed out “the potential for covariances to be introduced by the superimposition (or even just the spacing of the landmarks). There may also be covariances introduced or removed by the combine.subsets function.”

I found that all the models that I fit were favored over the null, and some models were also favored over others when fit to the simulated data.  If you also find that covariances are introduced by superimposition, and either introduced or removed by combining subsets, you might reconsider what the appropriate null hypothesis should be when testing for modularity.”

Dear all,

I have procrustes data from five different groups from the same genera (2 modern and 3 fossil populations) described with 13 fixed landmarks and 20 semi-landmarks, and I'm trying to test the difference between each group using procD.lm function.
The size of the group are the following : 252, 61, 26, 22 and 11 specimens.

Since there are very imbalanced group sizes with less than 30 specimens for some populations, I'm using the Goodal's F test with a simple factor as suggested in the help file of the function, followed by a pairwise comparison to see the differences among each pair of group.

The results show a significative difference among all groups, with the following scores:

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of raw values (residuals of mean)
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

           Df     SS       MS   Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)
genera      4 0.2486 0.062151 0.162 17.737 11.562  0.001 **
Residuals 367 1.2859 0.003504 0.838
Total     371 1.5346
---

And when I run the pairwise comparison, all sites pairs show statistically significant differences.
I am worried that two elements are bringing error:
- the imbalance dataset
- the high number of variables (13 landmarks, 20 semi-landmarks) despite having small populations.

My question is the following, do you think these problems might have an impact on the analysis, and if yes, how can I address it?

I tried to do the same analysis using PC scores to have a data-reduction, but the function procD.lm is not suited for that and I did not find any good alternative way to do a Goodal'F test on R.

Thank you for your help !

Louis

messages.body_plain:
Louis,

Data reduction to the set of PC dimensions that total 100% of the variation will yield identical results to what you are doing now. The reason is that under the hood, procD.lm using the trace of the SSCP matrices (think sum of variances). These will not change if redundant dimensions are embedded within the data, or if they are ‘spun out’ via PCA.

Also, and as a side-note, one can use procD.lm (or lm.rrpp) on non-landmark data like PCs. The function will accommodate either landmark data as a 3D array, or any data as a 2D matrix.

Dean

The results show a significative difference among all groups, with the following scores:

Dear Louis,

I have some things to add to Dean’s comments.

1. Contrary to your comment, procD.lm does in fact do a Goodall’s F-test (much more efficiently than some alternatives).  Here is some code to show this, using procD.lm and testmeanshapes from the shapes package, which allows a two-mean shape difference to be tested in painfully slow fashion.  I used the geomorph::pupfish data, which like your data has more shape variables than specimens.  (Note that the Goodall’s F is called G in this test.)

 library(geomorph)
> data("pupfish")
>
> fit <- procD.lm(coords~Sex, data = pupfish)
> anova(fit)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization

Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals

Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

          Df       SS        MS     Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)

Sex        1 0.015780 0.0157802 0.28012 20.235 4.3947  0.001 **
Residuals 52 0.040553 0.0007799 0.71988
Total     53 0.056333
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: procD.lm(f1 = coords ~ Sex, data = pupfish)
>
> coords.by.sex <- coords.subset(pupfish$coords, pupfish$Sex)
>
> library(shapes)
> testmeanshapes(coords.by.sex[[1]],
+                coords.by.sex[[2]],
+                resamples = 99) # this is too slow for many permutations
*Permutations - sampling without replacement: No of permutations =  99
***************************************************************************************************
$H
[1] 0.2992616

$H.pvalue
[1] 0.01

$H.table.pvalue
[1] 0.92671

$G
[1] 20.23581

$G.pvalue
[1] 0.01

$G.table.pvalue
[1] 0

$J
[1] 792.5643

$J.pvalue
[1] 0.01

$J.table.pvalue
[1] 0

As you can see, the F-stat via anova and procD.lm is the same as the G-stat, and the P-values are comparable (did not have patience to wait minutes for 1,000 random permutations in shapes when they were done in less than 1 second in geomorph).

2. You worry about imbalance but to my way of thinking, imbalance is more of an experimental design issue.  If one were assigning, for example, offspring from families to experimental treatments in a quantitative genetics design, having more individuals excessively representing few families in certain treatments could cause confounding issues between treatments and families.  I think you should be concerned more so with sampling error.  Small sample sizes could mean misrepresentation of the population from which you sample (genus).  There is no way to overcome this with statistical analysis — its an estimation problem.  Using reduced dimensions will not help remove sampling error or sampling bias.  You could put confidence ellipses around your mean shapes and they might be rather inflated for small samples, which is actually helpful for not interpreting inter-genus differences as meaningful if there is a lot of overlap.  (See RRPP::predict.lm.rrpp for examples.)

3. You should maybe consult our 2015 paper:

Collyer, M.L., D.J. Sekora, and D.C. Adams. 2015. A method for analysis of phenotypic change for phenotypes described by high-dimensional data. Heredity. 115:357-365.

This paper, along with several we have published since, demonstrate that using more shape dimensions rather than fewer can increase the ability (statistical power) to detect differences among groups.  You do have an effect size of 11.563 standard deviations for genera, so maybe your standards are a bit high?  You might lack an ability to discern differences with your low-sampled genera, but finding a method like dimension reduction that provides the significant results you would like is not an appropriate solution, if that even works.  It is statistical chicanery.

Best,
Mike

Hi all!

I have some questions about the output of bilat.symmetry.

I have two explanatory (ecological, taxonomic, and genetic) variables with many levels. I performed the bilat.symmetry function for each of the combinations mentioned above and, I suspect, directional asymmetry was significant in some combinations.

Now, I want to test the effect of ecological, taxonomic, and genetic variables on the magnitude of fluctuating asymmetry. However, the asymmetry index of bilat.symmetry represents both directional and fluctuating asymmetry (right?). Klingenberg (2015) stated that we can remove the effect of directional asymmetry to obtain a fluctuating asymmetry index. How can I do this with geomorph?

The reference paper of the bilat.symmetry function (Lazic et al., 2015) point out that “the square root of sums of squared differences from all landmark coordinates” is a fluctuating asymmetry index. However, I don’t understand how directional asymmetry was removed there.

Thanks in advance.

Best regards,

Juan

Klingenberg, C. P. (2015). Analyzing fluctuating asymmetry with geometric morphometrics: concepts, methods, and applications. Symmetry, 7(2), 843-934.

Lazić, M. M., Carretero, M. A., Crnobrnja-Isailović, J., & Kaliontzopoulou, A. (2015). Effects of environmental disturbance on phenotypic variation: an integrated assessment of canalization, developmental stability, modularity, and allometry in lizard head shape. The American Naturalist, 185(1), 44-58.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Juan,

fluctuating asymmetry is a pattern across a population, where individual asymmetry follows a normal distribution centered in zero, i.e. most individuals are symmetric and fairly equal numbers of individuals are asymmetric towards one side or the other. This kind of pattern is diagnosed as a significant interaction between individual and side in the typical ANOVA design done to test for asymmetry patterns (where the side effect alone, without a significant interaction, would suggest the existence of directional asymmetry).

The individual asymmetry indices one can derive to describe the magnitude of asymmetry and related it to other factors, can be signed (in that it tells you whether each individual is asymmetric towards the left or the right) or unsigned, where all signs of asymmetry are flipped towards one side and only the magnitude matters. Whether signed or unsigned indices make more sense biologically, and what would be the predictions and interpretation of variation in these indices is a matter of the researcher´s decision and view. At any rate, directional vs. fluctuating asymmetry PATTERN is not to be confused (nor does it really relate, conceptually) with signed vs. unsigned asymmetry INDEX. The mention in Lazic et al 2015 of any index as one of fluctuating asymmetry is an inaccurate wording.

Hope this helps
Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
If you use the parser function, you don't have to worry your landmarks are saved in JSON format. All you have to specify is the log file from SlicerMorph's GPA module, and it will read it into R as a 3D array of LM coordinates that geomorph and other shape analysis packages commonly expects.

If parser doesn't work, or for some reason you want to do this manually, you can also do that. Here is the snippet to read a single markup JSON file from Slicer. Replace the file path with any one of yours. Then you can loop over the files in that folder and add to this array (possibly using abind).

if (!require(SlicerMorphR)) {
  if (!require(devtools)) install.packages('devtools')
  devtools::install_github("SlicerMorph/SlicerMorphR")
}

library(SlicerMorphR)

LM = read.markups.json("C:/users/murat/Documents/F.mrk.json")
LM

As for your second question, see Dean's response above. If that example doesn't help, you might actually benefit attending a workshop or short-course focused on theory behind statistical shape analysis.

messages.body_plain:
You 'can' create a species ID table in Slicer and save it as as csv file along with the rest of your data, but you will have to manually import into R (it won't be part of parser functionality). So, it is as easy and probably more contained (from data management) to do in the way you did. Just make sure imported files and your species classifiers are in the same order.
